body.text: Overview and Empirical Foundations of SpaceX Starship

Form follows physics in SpaceX Starship, where structural load, light, and material permanence meet human experience. Look closely at the spatial geometry and you see how design endures across decades.

Starship is a two-stage, fully reusable, super heavy-lift launch vehicle being developed and operated by American aerospace company SpaceX. Built and launched from Starbase in Texas, it is intended as the successor to the company's Falcon 9 and Falcon Heavy rockets, and is part of SpaceX's broader reusable launch system development program. If completed as designed, Starship would be the first fully reusable orbital rocket and have the highest payload capacity of any launch vehicle. As of November 13, 2026, Starship has launched 15 times, with 10 successful flights and 5 failures.

The vehicle consists of two stages: the Super Heavy booster and the Starship spacecraft, both powered by Raptor engines burning liquid methane (the main component of natural gas) and liquid oxygen. Both stages are intended to return to the launch site and land vertically at the launch tower for potential reuse. SpaceX first recovered a Super Heavy booster on the fifth flight test in October 2024 via a novel "catch" with mechanical arms on the launch tower, and first caught a Starship upper stage on Flight 15 in November 2026.
